items.title: Fix NAX tile bugs and make the gather_qmm block tile tunable
items.body:
## Proposed changes

A mixture of experts layer calls the NAX kernel for `gather_qmm` during
prefill, and that kernel is built for a single block tile: 64,64,64,2,2. The
block tile has a large effect on how fast the kernel runs, but you cannot
change it, because two bugs stop you as soon as you try.

This pull request lets you tune the block tile, and corrects both bugs.

### Why the block tile matters

Each threadgroup handles a range of rows, and the rows arrive sorted by
expert. A threadgroup that starts in one expert and ends in the next must
repeat its whole K loop for the second expert, so a block tile with fewer rows
produces fewer threadgroups that cross a boundary.

We measured this on a mixture of experts prefill shape, where M is 20480, K is
3072, N is 2048, and there are 256 experts. The weights use affine
quantization with 2 bits and a group size of 128. The machine is an M5 Max.

| Rows in the block tile | Speed |
|---|---|
| 128 | 0.73x |
| 64 (the default, 8.85 ms) | 1.00x |
| 32 (8.13 ms) | 1.09x |
| 16 | 0.83x |

A block tile with 32 rows takes the full layer from 13.17 ms to 12.12 ms,
which is 8 percent, and makes end to end prefill 2 to 5 percent faster.

The best block tile differs between models, and it also depends on how many
rows each expert receives, so this pull request does not change the default.
It builds the kernel for 6 block tiles, and the environment variable
`MLX_QMM_TILE_NAX` selects one of them in the format `"BM,BN,BK,WM,WN"`.
`quantized.cpp` reads the variable with `env::get_var` at dispatch time, in
the same way that `scaled_dot_product_attention.cpp` reads `MLX_SDPA_BLOCKS`.
If the value is not one of the 6 block tiles, MLX raises an error that lists
the ones you can use.

The kernel for hardware without NAX behaves the same way, and it already
carries a `TODO: Tune the block sizes` comment. A rule that picks the block
tile from the shape would help both kernels, and this pull request gives you
the tool to measure such a rule.

### The first bug: the block loader accepts one shape

The block loader dequantizes the weights into threadgroup memory, but it
accepted only a block tile no wider than one quantization group. A second copy
of the loader handled the special case of a group size of 32, and that copy
contained this line:

```
static_assert(..., "Other configurations are not yet supported");
```

Every new block tile stops there first.

The first commit merges all the cases into one loader and deletes the copy. A
thread can now read less than one quantization group, part of one group, or
several whole groups. The block tiles that MLX builds today still take the
path they took before.

### The second bug: the matmul does nothing

`tile_matmad_nax` used the M paired path when `TN == 1 && TM % 2 == 0`, and
the N paired path when `TN % 2 == 0`, but it had no other case. A block tile
with an odd `TN` matched neither, so the body of the function was empty: the
matmul never ran, and the output tile kept the zeros that `clear()` wrote. The
kernel still compiled and still ran, and it looked much faster than it was.

You can see this without building MLX. Put this file in the root of the
repository:

```cpp
// probe.metal
#include "mlx/backend/metal/kernels/utils.h"
#include "mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/gemm/nax.h"
using namespace mlx::steel;

kernel void probe(device float* out [[buffer(0)]]) {
  NAXTile<float, 1, 1> C;          // TM is 1, TN is 1
  NAXTile<bfloat16_t, 1, 2> A;     // TK is 2
  NAXTile<bfloat16_t, 2, 1> B;
  C.clear(); A.clear(); B.clear();
  tile_matmad_nax(C, A, metal::bool_constant<false>{},
                     B, metal::bool_constant<false>{});
  out[0] = C.val_frags[0][0];
}
```

Then count the matmul instructions:

```
xcrun metal -c probe.metal -I . -S -o out.air
grep -c "matmul\|mma" out.air
```

On main this prints **0**, and with the second commit it prints **41**.

The same commit corrects the descriptor of the M paired fragment matmul. That
overload takes 2 fragments along M and 1 fragment along N, so the problem is
32x16x16, but the code built the descriptor as
`matmul2d_descriptor(16, 32, 16)`, which is the shape of the N paired
overload. The copy into the left input tensor then ran past the end of that
tensor.

The block tile that MLX selects today reaches neither bug, but any other block
tile reaches both.

### Tests

`test_gather_qmm_rhs_nax_tiles` in `python/tests/test_quantized.py` calls
`gather_qmm` with all 6 block tiles, at a group size of 32 and of 64, and with
a row count that divides the rows of the block tile as well as one that does
not. It compares every result against `dequantize` followed by `gather_mm`,
and it checks that an unknown block tile raises an error. The test skips on
hardware without matrix coprocessors.

Two of the 6 block tiles give each simdgroup a single fragment along N, so
they take the paths that the second commit corrects, and the group size of 32
makes one row of a block tile span several quantization groups, which is the
case the first commit adds.

These are the results on an M5 Max with macOS 26.5:

- `test_quantized.py`: 34 tests, all pass.
- `test_blas.py`: 28 tests, all pass.
- If you remove the second commit, the new test fails on exactly the block
  tiles that give one fragment along N, because the kernel returns zeros.
- If you remove the first commit, `quantized_nax.metal` does not compile.

The `gather_qmm` docstring documents `MLX_QMM_TILE_NAX`.

## Checklist

Put an `x` in the boxes that apply.

- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) document
- [x] I have run `pre-commit run --all-files` to format my code / installed pre-commit prior to committing changes
- [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works
- [x] I have updated the necessary documentation (if needed)

items.title: [BUG] Metal 2-pass vector SDPA kernel produces garbage decode output on M3 Max (applegpu_g15s) with GQA once KV length reaches 1024
items.body:
### Describe the bug

On an M3 Max (`applegpu_g15s`), single-token decode routed to
`sdpa_vector_2pass` produces numerically wrong output for a GQA model
(32 query heads / 8 KV heads, head_dim 128). Generation is correct for every
step routed to the 1-pass `sdpa_vector` kernel and collapses into a runaway of
`!` tokens starting at exactly the first step whose KV length reaches the
2-pass routing threshold of 1024.

The dispatch site is `mlx/backend/metal/scaled_dot_product_attention.cpp`
(lines 740–750 at `ce45c52`, tag `v0.31.1`):

```cpp
// We route to the 2 pass fused attention if
// - The device is large and the sequence length long
// - The sequence length is even longer and we have gqa
bool do_causal = do_causal_ && q.shape(2) > 1;
char devc = d.get_architecture().back();
if (((devc == 'd' || devc == 's') && k.shape(2) >= 1024) ||
    (k.shape(1) < q.shape(1) && k.shape(2) >= 4096)) {
  sdpa_vector_2pass(s, d, q, k, v, o, scale_, do_causal, mask, sinks);
} else {
  sdpa_vector(s, d, q, k, v, o, scale_, do_causal, mask, sinks);
}
```

`applegpu_g15s` ends in `'s'`, so the first condition fires at `k.shape(2) == 1024`.

I have **not** isolated the fault inside the 2-pass kernel itself. What I can
show is that the failure is exactly co-located with this dispatch decision:
forcing every vector-path decode onto `sdpa_vector` makes the output correct,
with nothing else changed.

For this configuration `sdpa_vector_2pass` selects `blocks = 64` (device char
`'s'`, `n_simds = gqa_factor * q.shape(2) = 4 * 1 = 4`, so the `n_simds > 4`
escalation does not apply), `BN = 32`, `head_dim = 128`.

### To reproduce

I do not have a standalone pure-MLX numeric repro — the failure was found and
pinned in a Swift VLM generation stack. I can build a minimal one on request if
that would help; the setup below is 100% deterministic and reproduces every run.

1. Stack: `mlx-swift` (Cmlx core pinned at `ce45c52` = `v0.31.1`) +
   `ml-explore/mlx-swift-lm` at `3cbf928b5eb24190e8952725699ae6a3bb02824d`,
   using `MLXVLM` / `MLXLMCommon`.
2. Model: `mlx-community/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct-4bit` (affine, 4 bits, group 64).
   Text config: 36 layers, `num_attention_heads: 32`, `num_key_value_heads: 8`,
   `head_dim: 128`, `hidden_size: 4096`.
3. Single image + short instruction prompt, sized so that vision tokens +
   prompt land a few hundred tokens *below* 1024 (mine: a 1404x1872 page image
   with the pixel budget clamped to 786,432, giving a prompt KV of 905).
4. `GenerateParameters(maxTokens: 1024, temperature: 0)`. Default KV cache —
   `KVCacheSimple`, `maxKVSize` unset, so no rotation and no cache-side
   quantization. Nothing in my configuration is parameterized at 1024.
5. Generate.

With an instrumented build printing `k.shape(2)`, `q.shape(1)`, `k.shape(1)`
and the branch taken at the dispatch site, the run produces:

```
[SDPA_ROUTE] kv=1022 qh=32 kvh=8 -> 1pass
[SDPA_ROUTE] kv=1023 qh=32 kvh=8 -> 1pass
[SDPA_ROUTE] kv=1024 qh=32 kvh=8 -> 2pass
[SDPA_ROUTE] kv=1024 qh=32 kvh=8 -> 2pass
```

with 4,284 `1pass` calls and 32,580 `2pass` calls. 4,284 / 36 layers = 119
decode steps, and 905 + 119 = 1024 — i.e. every step before the routing flip is
1-pass, every step from the flip onward is 2-pass.

The generated text has exactly 119 sensible tokens followed by 904 `!` tokens
(1,023 total against `maxTokens: 1024`), so the collapse begins on the very
first token computed by the 2-pass kernel.

The collapse point tracks KV length, not content: with a different image /
prompt length the clean prefix grows or shrinks so that the break still lands
at cumulative KV 1024.

### Expected behavior

`sdpa_vector_2pass` and `sdpa_vector` produce the same output (within fp
tolerance), so crossing the routing threshold mid-generation is invisible.

### Actual behavior

Output is correct up to the routing flip and then degenerates immediately into
a `!`/whitespace runaway that continues until the token budget is exhausted.
Sanitized shape of the transcript (content replaced, structure preserved):

```
- [ ] first item, transcribed correctly
- [ ] second item, transcribed correctly
...
- [ ] Check if Ju(!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
  (904 '!' tokens, to the token limit)
```

It cuts in mid-word, at temperature 0 — this is not a sampling artifact, and
`!` is the token the logits collapse onto.

### Environment

- macOS 26.5.1 (build 25F80)
- MacBook Pro, `Mac15,9`, Apple M3 Max, 16-core CPU, 48 GB unified memory
- Metal GPU architecture: `applegpu_g15s` (so `devc == 's'`)
- mlx core `v0.31.1` (`ce45c52`), consumed as the `Cmlx` submodule of
  `ml-explore/mlx-swift`
- `ml-explore/mlx-swift-lm` @ `3cbf928b5eb24190e8952725699ae6a3bb02824d`
- Model: `mlx-community/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct-4bit`

### Additional context

**Workaround (2-line dispatch patch).** Raising both routing thresholds out of
reach forces the vector path onto the 1-pass kernel and fixes the output
completely:

```diff
@@ -742,8 +742,8 @@ void ScaledDotProductAttention::eval_gpu(
-    if (((devc == 'd' || devc == 's') && k.shape(2) >= 1024) ||
-        (k.shape(1) < q.shape(1) && k.shape(2) >= 4096)) {
+    if (((devc == 'd' || devc == 's') && k.shape(2) >= 100000000) ||
+        (k.shape(1) < q.shape(1) && k.shape(2) >= 100000000)) {
       sdpa_vector_2pass(s, d, q, k, v, o, scale_, do_causal, mask, sinks);
     } else {
       sdpa_vector(s, d, q, k, v, o, scale_, do_causal, mask, sinks);
```

Branch: https://github.com/byndsim/mlx/tree/markink/sdpa-1pass
(commit `d8964f06ae1d4b0f856bfb4d4b4a9437cf9b77ed`, based on `ce45c52`).

With that patch, the same 22 inputs run clean over a long-KV batch, verified to
a maximum KV length of 6,022 with zero 2-pass dispatches and no `!` runaway on
any page. This is obviously not a fix — it forfeits the 2-pass kernel's
long-context performance — but it does localize the fault to the 2-pass path.

**Not fixed in v0.32.0.** I diffed `v0.31.1..v0.32.0`:

- `mlx/backend/metal/kernels/sdpa_vector.h` is byte-identical (empty diff), so
  both 2-pass kernel bodies are unchanged.
- `scaled_dot_product_attention.cpp` changed (15 insertions / 11 deletions) but
  the two routing thresholds are untouched; the changes are the
  `metal::get_command_encoder(s)` refactor, a 192/128 head-dim allowance in
  `use_fallback`, and a new `MLX_SDPA_BLOCKS` env override in
  `sdpa_vector_2pass`. The `blocks` selection logic itself is unchanged.

I have not tested v0.32.0 end-to-end (the version bump does not build against
the mlx-c revision my Swift stack pins), so this is a source-level rather than
a runtime finding.

The new `MLX_SDPA_BLOCKS` knob in 0.32.0 may make this easy to bisect from
Python — if the failure turns out to be block-count-dependent, that would also
explain why Python users on the same hardware might not have hit it (I have not
been able to confirm either way; I have no Python mlx install on this machine).

**Still present on current `main` (source-level, checked 2026-08-05):** the
2-pass routing thresholds and the `blocks` selection heuristic in
`scaled_dot_product_attention.cpp` are structurally unchanged from `v0.31.1`,
and `sdpa_vector.h`'s 2-pass kernel bodies likewise. I see #4018 is currently
touching the 1-pass `sdpa_vector` dispatch (threadgroup-size check), so this
area is active — happy to rebase my instrumentation onto whatever lands there.
Possibly-related numerics reports I found while searching (neither matches this
failure shape): #3585 (fused-vs-manual float ordering, with a Metal-toolchain
theory) and #3856 (M5 quantized-MoE corruption).

**Offer:** I ship this workaround in a production app and maintain a
deterministic RED/GREEN regression test for it (a whole-page VLM transcription
that runs KV well past 1024 and asserts a clean, non-degenerate result — RED on
the stock kernel, GREEN with the dispatch patch, runs in under a minute with
weights installed). I'm glad to run that gate against candidate fixes on the
affected M3-class hardware, provide the full instrumented routing log and exact
prompt/image setup, or build a minimal standalone repro against Python mlx —
just say which is most useful.

items.title: quantized_matmul does not amortize the weight read for small M, while the bf16 path does
items.body:
# quantized_matmul does not amortize the weight read for small M, while the bf16 path does

## Summary

`mx.quantized_matmul` scales close to linearly in `M` for `M` in 2..8, where the
dense bf16 path is flat. The weight read appears not to be amortized across rows
until roughly `M >= 16`. Since speculative decoding, multi-token draft
verification, and small-batch serving all live in `M = 2..8`, this shows up
directly in end-to-end decode throughput on quantized models.

## Measurement

M3 Ultra (512 GB), mlx 0.31.2 and 0.32.0 — identical results on both.
Shape `(M, 5120) @ (17408, 5120)^T`, `group_size=64`. Timings are queue-batched
(64 ops enqueued per `mx.eval`) to stay above the per-call sync floor; a
per-call `mx.eval` puts every entry near ~0.25 ms and hides the effect entirely.

| M | bf16 ms | vs M=1 | 4-bit ms | vs M=1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.271 | 1.00x | 0.041 | 1.00x |
| 2 | 0.539 | 1.99x | 0.076 | 1.83x |
| 4 | 0.538 | **1.99x** | 0.134 | 3.26x |
| 7 | 0.539 | **1.99x** | 0.218 | **5.28x** |
| 8 | 0.541 | 2.00x | 0.252 | 6.12x |
| 16 | 0.541 | 2.00x | 0.260 | 6.32x |

bf16 is flat from M=2 onward — one weight read serves every row. The 4-bit path
grows almost linearly to M=8 and only then saturates. 8-bit behaves the same
way, and additionally shows M=16 (0.264 ms) landing *below* M=8 (0.378 ms),
which looks like a path switch at 16.

Against a roofline — weights read once at a measured 677 GB/s, compute at ~20
TFLOPS — M=7 should cost about 0.074 ms:

| M | ideal ms | 4-bit ms | vs ideal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.074 | 0.041 | 0.51x |
| 4 | 0.074 | 0.134 | 1.62x |
| 7 | 0.074 | 0.204 | 2.75x |

M=1 is at roofline. M=7 is 2.75x off it.

## Why it matters

The whole-model effect on a 27B hybrid (Qwen3.8-27B, 4-bit, 48 GatedDeltaNet +
16 full-attention layers), timing one forward at sequence length S:

| S | ms | vs roofline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 29.7 | 1.41x |
| 4 | 45.4 | 2.15x |
| 7 | 62.5 | 2.96x |
| 8 | 77.1 | **3.65x** |
| 32 | 105.4 | 1.44x |
| 128 | 347.9 | 1.19x |

Efficiency is worst exactly in the speculative-decoding window and recovers at
large S. I ruled out the linear-attention kernel as the cause: benchmarked
alone it is flat from T=1 to T=64 (0.28-0.37 ms), because it keeps its recurrent
state in registers across the time loop.

Concretely, this decides whether speculative decoding is viable at all. With a
draft model reaching an acceptance length of 2.5 at block size 7, verification
currently costs 62.5 ms per step and the scheme runs at 1.03x of plain decode —
i.e. not worth doing. If the batched forward cost tracked the roofline the way
M=1 does, verification would be ~30 ms and the same drafter would give ~1.9x.
A third party reports 1.66x for this exact model and drafter on the same
hardware through a different stack, which is consistent with that estimate.

## What I tried

I wrote a Metal kernel that reads each quantized weight group once and reuses it
across all M rows, with x staged in threadgroup memory and per-group x-sums
precomputed for the bias term. It reproduces `quantized_matmul` to bf16 output
precision (max relative deviation 7e-3), and the scaling does improve — 4.84x at
M=8 versus MLX's 6.15x — but the absolute cost is 2.6-3.3x worse than MLX
because the scalar inner loop and threadgroup traffic swamp the saving. Getting
the remaining 2.75x plainly needs a `simdgroup_matrix` formulation, which is
where the existing M>=16 path presumably already is; the gap looks like small M
falling off that path rather than anything fundamental.

## Reproduction

```python
import time
import mlx.core as mx

N, K = 17408, 5120

def bench(M, bits, reps=64, iters=6):
    x = mx.random.normal((M, K)).astype(mx.bfloat16)
    w = mx.random.normal((N, K)).astype(mx.bfloat16)
    if bits is None:
        wt = mx.contiguous(w.T)
        mx.eval(x, wt)
        run = lambda: mx.eval([x @ wt for _ in range(reps)])
    else:
        wq, s, b = mx.quantize(w, group_size=64, bits=bits)
        mx.eval(x, wq, s, b)
        run = lambda: mx.eval([
            mx.quantized_matmul(x, wq, s, b, transpose=True, group_size=64, bits=bits)
            for _ in range(reps)
        ])
    run()
    mx.synchronize()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(iters):
        run()
    mx.synchronize()
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / iters / reps * 1000

for label, bits in (("bf16", None), ("4-bit", 4)):
    base = bench(1, bits)
    print(label, [f"M={M}: {bench(M, bits)/base:.2f}x" for M in (2, 4, 7, 8, 16)])
```

## Environment

- M3 Ultra, 512 GB, macOS 15 (Darwin 25.5.0)
- mlx 0.31.2 and 0.32.0 — same numbers on both

items.title: Silent numerical corruption in single long forward on quantized MoE when sequence length % 32 != 0 (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-8bit, M5)
items.body:
## Summary

A single `model(ids)` forward over a long prompt on a quantized MoE model
produces silently corrupted activations/KV whenever the forward's sequence
length is **not a multiple of 32**. Feeding the identical token ids through
the identical model in 2048-token chunks (what `mlx_lm.generate_step` does)
gives a different — and behaviorally correct — result. The divergence is
deterministic, content-independent (reproduces with random token ids), large
(fp16 K-cache entries off by up to ~86; final-position logits off by ~17–23;
greedy argmax flips), and big enough to break downstream behavior: a
needle-in-haystack QA that scores 100% recall with chunked prefill scores 0%
with a one-shot prefill at N≈16k.

This looks like a sibling of the 0.31.x quantized-matmul alignment bugs
(`gather_qmm` >32k-row MoE corruption; unaligned-N `quantized_matmul` with
m ≥ 10, m % 32 ≠ 0 — both fixed in 0.32.0). The MoE expert path appears to
still have an unaligned-M case: dense models (Qwen3-8B/32B, same quant
recipes, same lengths) are behaviorally clean in the same A/B, and the first
divergent tensor we observe is layer 1's K — i.e. the corruption enters
through layer 0's block output. Since dense models exercise the same
attention path at these shapes cleanly, the MoE FFN (`gather_qmm` /
gather-QMM-family kernels) is the prime suspect.

## Environment

- mlx **0.32.0.dev20260708+1ac2fbac** and **0.32.1.dev20260715+cf3ce39c**
  (both reproduce; source builds with NAX kernels enabled,
  `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=26.2`)
- Apple M5, macOS 26 (Darwin 25.5.0), Python 3.12
- Model: `mlx-community/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-8bit` (affine 8-bit,
  MoE 30B-A3B). Dense `mlx-community/Qwen3-8B-4bit` / `Qwen3-32B-4bit` do
  **not** reproduce behaviorally at the same lengths.
- mlx-lm used only to load the model and build the KV cache.

## Repro

```python
# python repro.py            -> single length
# python repro.py --bisect   -> alignment scan
import argparse
import mlx.core as mx
from mlx_lm import load
from mlx_lm.models.cache import make_prompt_cache

def cache_diff(model, ids, chunk=2048):
    def build(step):
        cache = make_prompt_cache(model)
        for s in range(0, len(ids), step):
            logits = model(mx.array([ids[s:s+step]]), cache=cache)
            mx.eval(logits, [c.state for c in cache])
        return cache, logits[0, -1]
    c1, l1 = build(len(ids))   # one-shot
    c2, l2 = build(chunk)      # chunked
    worst_k = 0.0
    for a, b in zip(c1, c2):
        if getattr(a, "keys", None) is None:
            continue
        n = min(a.offset, b.offset)
        dk = float(mx.max(mx.abs(a.state[0][..., :n, :] - b.state[0][..., :n, :])).item())
        worst_k = max(worst_k, dk)
    dl = float(mx.max(mx.abs(l1 - l2)).item())
    same = int(mx.argmax(l1).item()) == int(mx.argmax(l2).item())
    return worst_k, dl, same

ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
ap.add_argument("--model", default="mlx-community/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-8bit")
ap.add_argument("--bisect", action="store_true")
args = ap.parse_args()

model, tok = load(args.model)
mx.random.seed(0)
ids = mx.random.randint(0, 50000, (17000,)).tolist()
lengths = [8192, 12288, 16000, 16032, 16064, 16065, 16066, 16067, 16068,
           16128, 16384, 16900] if args.bisect else [16068]
print(f"mlx {mx.__version__}")
print(f"{'N':>7} {'worstK':>8} {'logitdiff':>9}  argmax")
for L in lengths:
    wk, dl, ok = cache_diff(model, ids[:L], 2048)
    print(f"{L:>7} {wk:>8.3f} {dl:>9.3f}  {'OK' if ok else 'DIVERGED'}", flush=True)
```

## Observed (random ids, seed 0, deterministic across runs)

```
mlx 0.32.0.dev20260708+1ac2fbac        (0.32.1.dev20260715: same pattern)
      N   worstK logitdiff  argmax
   8192   15.125     0.562  OK          # 32-aligned
  12288   15.125     1.172  OK          # 32-aligned
  16000   15.125     0.182  OK          # 32-aligned
  16032   15.125     0.344  OK          # 32-aligned
  16064   26.000     0.109  OK          # 32-aligned
  16065   32.000     7.562  DIVERGED    # N % 32 == 1
  16066   32.500     8.312  DIVERGED    # N % 32 == 2
  16067   32.000     8.375  DIVERGED    # N % 32 == 3
  16068   32.000    17.500  DIVERGED    # N % 32 == 4
  16128   26.000     1.148  OK          # 32-aligned
  16384   26.000     0.188  OK          # 32-aligned
  16900   32.000     9.438  DIVERGED    # N % 32 == 4
```

Every diverging length is unaligned; every 32-aligned length matches argmax
with small logit deltas. Unaligned lengths below 16k already show large
numeric error without flipping the argmax at the final position (e.g. on
0.32.1.dev20260715: N=8193 → worstK 131, logitdiff 17.0, argmax OK; N=12289 →
worstK 54, logitdiff 4.3, argmax OK), so short-prompt spot checks miss it.

Notes:

- The constant worstK ≈ 15–26 at aligned lengths is presumably benign
  kernel-tiling numerics amplified by outlier channels (argmax stable, logit
  deltas ≪ 1 in most rows); the unaligned case is qualitatively different.
- Layer-0 K is identical between the two paths (it depends only on the
  embeddings); divergence first appears in layer-1 K and compounds through
  all 48 layers.
- Real-workload impact: with a real 16,068-token needle-in-haystack prompt,
  the one-shot path's K diverges by up to 86, final logits by 23.4, and
  greedy QA recall flips 1.0 → 0.0 (the model emits repetitive
  off-task text). Chunked prefill of the same ids answers correctly. This
  cost us a multi-day false negative in a KV-eviction study before we traced
  it to the prefill path.

## Workaround

Chunk all prefills (any chunk size that keeps each forward 32-aligned or
short works; we use 2048).

We can test candidate fixes, run finer-grained bisects, or collect kernel-level
traces on M5 hardware on request.

items.title: [BUG] Metal GPU watchdog kills LoRA training when display is active
items.body:
**Describe the bug**

LoRA fine-tuning crashes with `kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorImpactingInteractivity` when the laptop display is active. The macOS Metal GPU watchdog kills the training process because GPU command buffers from MLX block WindowServer display compositing. The crash is 100% reproducible with the display on (4/4 runs across macOS 26.2 and 26.3.1) and 100% avoidable with the display off (closing the lid with `caffeinate -s` to prevent sleep, this eliminates WindowServer GPU compositing, so the watchdog's "impacting interactivity" check has nothing to protect and never fires).

The workload is minimal: 2.75GB peak memory on a 16GB system (17% utilization), batch_size=1, max_seq_length=256, every parameter at or more conservative than mlx-lm defaults.

**To Reproduce**

```bash
pip install mlx-lm

# Training data: 105 JSONL chat examples, ~256 tokens each
# (Qwen format with system/user/assistant messages containing <think> + <tool_call> blocks)
# Short examples (~40 tokens, ~3.0 it/sec) do NOT crash
# Long examples (~256 tokens, ~0.8 it/sec) crash every time

python -m mlx_lm lora \
  --model mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-OptiQ-4bit \
  --train --data ./data \
  --config lora_config.yaml \
  --adapter-path ./adapters

# Crashes within 1-5 minutes:
# libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::runtime_error:
# [METAL] Command buffer execution failed: Impacting Interactivity
# (0000000e:kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorImpactingInteractivity)
```

lora_config.yaml:
```yaml
model: mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-OptiQ-4bit
fine_tune_type: lora
batch_size: 1
num_layers: 8
lora_parameters:
  rank: 8
  scale: 20.0
  dropout: 0.0
iters: 500
steps_per_eval: 500
learning_rate: 1e-5
grad_checkpoint: true
mask_prompt: true
max_seq_length: 256
```

Results across 5 runs:

| Run | macOS | Display | Background | Result |
|-----|-------|---------|-----------|--------|
| 1 | 26.2 | Open | Minimal | Crashed iter ~180 |
| 2 | 26.2 | Open | Normal OS activity | Crashed iter ~53 |
| 3 | 26.2 | Open | Normal OS activity | Crashed iter ~43 |
| 4 | 26.3.1 | Open | Normal OS activity | Crashed iter ~1 |
| **5** | **26.3.1** | **Closed** | **caffeinate -s** | **Completed 500/500** |

**Expected behavior**

Training completes all 500 iterations. The workload uses 17% of available GPU memory with the most conservative possible settings.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
- OS Version: macOS 26.2 Tahoe and macOS 26.3.1 Tahoe
- MLX Version: 0.31.1
- mlx-lm Version: 0.31.1
- Hardware: MacBook Pro M2 Pro, 16GB unified memory
- Python: 3.14.3

**Additional context**

- `MLX_MAX_OPS_PER_BUFFER=1` and `MLX_MAX_MB_PER_BUFFER=10` do not prevent the crash with the display active
- Normal background OS activity and rendering windows accelerates the crash, more GPU contention from WindowServer compositing means earlier crashes
- The crash does not occur with short training examples (~40 tokens, 1.75GB peak, ~3.0 it/sec), only with longer sequences (~256 tokens, 2.75GB peak, ~0.8 it/sec) where individual GPU operations take ~1.2 seconds
- Workaround: `caffeinate -s &` then close the laptop lid. With no active display, WindowServer does not need GPU time for compositing, so the watchdog never triggers. Training completes normally.
- Training data and config available on request for reproduction

items.title: Make the gather_qmm_rhs dispatch thresholds overridable
items.body:
## The situation

`GatherQMM::eval_gpu` picks the batched `gather_qmm_rhs` path from two hard-coded thresholds that the code itself flags as unturned — `mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp`:

```cpp
  // TODO: Tune 16 and 4 here a bit better.
  if (M == 1 && B >= 16 && right_sorted_ == true && B / E >= 4) {
```

For MoE decode at batch size 1 with a large expert count, **both conditions are unsatisfiable regardless of how routing is distributed**, so the batched path can never be selected and never measured against.

Concretely, for a 35B-A3B-shaped model — 256 experts, top-8 routing, single-token decode:

```
M = 1                      (one token)
B = 8                      (8 gathered rows)
E = 256                    (experts)

B >= 16          ->  8 >= 16            false
B / E >= 4       ->  needs B >= 1024    false   (8/256 = 0)
```

`B / E` is an *average* rows-per-expert, so satisfying it needs 1024 gathered rows — 128 tokens at top-8. That is a batch-decode regime, not single-token decode. The threshold isn't merely conservative for this shape; it is unreachable.

I am not claiming the current defaults are wrong. I am claiming that with them hard-coded there is no way to find out, short of patching and rebuilding MLX — which is the position I am in, and why this is the first thing I would like to change.

## The change

Two `env::`-namespace accessors in `mlx/utils.h`, following the existing pattern used by `bfs_max_width`, `max_ops_per_buffer`, `metal_fast_synch`, `enable_tf32`, `nccl_timeout` and `metal_gpu_arch`:

- `MLX_GATHER_QMM_RHS_MIN_ROWS` — default **16**
- `MLX_GATHER_QMM_RHS_MIN_ROWS_PER_EXPERT` — default **4**

**Defaults are the previous hard-coded values, so behaviour is unchanged unless the environment says otherwise.** No kernel changes, no API changes, no new dependencies.

I also expanded the comment to record *why* the second condition behaves the way it does for large expert counts, since that is the part that surprised me.

### One thing I deliberately did not do

An earlier draft of mine rewrote `B / E >= 4` as `B >= 4 * E`, on the grounds that it reads better. The two are equivalent for positive integers, but once the multiplier is settable the product form can overflow `int` where the division form cannot, so I kept the division. Mentioning it in case the rewrite looks like an oversight.

## Evidence

- **Compiles clean.** I compiled the affected translation unit to an object using the compile command MLX's own CMake build recorded in `compile_commands.json` — exit 0, 273 KB object, **zero errors and zero warnings**. Also `-fsyntax-only`, exit 0, no diagnostics.
- **READ** `mlx/utils.cpp:253-259` — `get_var(const char*, int)` is `std::getenv` + `atoi` with a default fallback, so an unset variable yields exactly the previous constant.
- **READ** `mlx/utils.h:141-176` — the six existing accessors use the identical `static`-cached form; these two are written the same way.
- **Verified not stale:** the `TODO` comment and the dispatch condition are unchanged on `main` at `quantized.cpp:1586-1587` as of today.

**What I did not do, stated plainly:** I have not run a full `libmlx` build or an end-to-end A/B of the two dispatch paths. The A/B is the thing this PR unblocks — I cannot produce that number until the thresholds are reachable without a fork, which is the whole request. If you would rather see a full build plus benchmark numbers before merging, I am happy to do that; it just has to come after something like this lands, or against a temporary fork whose numbers you would reasonably discount.

## Why I want it

I am running a 35B-A3B MoE with experts streamed from SSD on a 24 GB Apple M4, and the per-expert quantized gather is the largest single term I have measured in the decode path. I would like to find out whether the batched path helps at `B = 8`, and at present I cannot ask the question. If the answer turns out to be "the defaults are right, the batched path is worse here", that is a useful result too — and I would be glad to send it back as a tuning follow-up with real numbers.

items.title: Add inverse-CDF path for large categorical sampling
items.body:
# PR: Add a transform-aware inverse-CDF path for large categorical sampling

## Summary

This change adds a source-level `CategoricalSearch` primitive and uses it to avoid
the `O(B*N*M)` Gumbel temporary created by
`random::categorical(logits, num_samples=M)` for large Metal workloads.

Fixes #3847.

The inverse-CDF path uses FP32 softmax probabilities rounded onto a 52-bit uint64
mass grid, an exact uint64 cumulative sum, one uint32 random word per output
sample, and a Metal binary search kernel. CPU and non-Metal backends retain the
existing Gumbel-max path.

## Why

Issue #3847 reports that drawing many samples from a large categorical creates a
Gumbel tensor with `B*N*M` elements. For `N=M=1,000,000`, that formulation would
require roughly 4 TB for the FP32 temporary.

A float32 inverse-CDF prototype reduced memory but failed an adversarial support
test: with one million categories and a 0.99 head probability, only 249,772 CDF
entries had positive increments. The uint64 fixed-point representation preserves
all one million positive weights.

## Implementation

- Add `CategoricalSearch(cdf[..., N], bits[..., M]) -> uint32[..., M]`.
- Add exact CPU evaluation for oracle testing.
- Add a Metal kernel using binary search and an overflow-safe 32x64 target map.
- Add an explicit vmap rule for both-mapped, CDF-only, and random-bits-only cases.
- Add export/import serialization.
- Normalize non-contiguous inputs inside backend evaluators so `Contiguous` does
  not leak into exported graphs.
- Define Metal-compatible non-finite behavior before the fixed-point cast:
  first `+inf` wins, NaNs are masked when another valid category exists, and
  rows containing only NaN/`-inf` choose category zero.
- Dispatch only on Metal for the `num_samples` overload when `B*N*M >= 2^19`.
  CPU, CUDA, complex logits, other overloads, and smaller workloads remain
  unchanged.
- Keep the source helpers in `random_impl.h` rather than adding experimental
  functions to the public C++ random API.

## Correctness

- CPU and Metal are bitwise identical for the same explicit CDF/random words.
- 1D/2D/3D batch and first/middle/last category axes pass.
- FP32/FP16/BF16/integer/bool logits follow an explicit FP32 softmax policy.
- direct, compile, vmap, compile-vmap, nested batched vmap, and export/import pass.
- Three-seed distribution test: max z-score 2.18, max TV 0.00139.
- One-million-category skew stress:
  - positive float CDF steps: 249,772;
  - positive fixed weights: 1,000,000;
  - fixed quantization TV: 4.94e-6;
  - tail z-score: 0.20.
- One-million-category uniform stress: max 32-bucket z-score 2.83.

## Performance (Apple M5)

31 interleaved paired measurements, bootstrap 95% CI:

| Workload | Median speedup | 95% CI | Peak-memory reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| B=8, N=M=1024 | 23.70x | [23.17, 24.56] | 75.12x |
| B=1, N=M=8000 | 156.56x | [148.44, 163.51] | 530.94x |

The final `2^19` guard selected 23 formal grid cases; all 23 had a paired-speedup
CI lower bound above 1.02. Source graph checks confirm that guard-outside and CPU
paths contain the stock `ArgReduce` graph and do not construct
`CategoricalSearch`.

## Compatibility and limitations

- The inverse-CDF path is deterministic for a given key but does not preserve
  Gumbel-max's exact random sequence.
- The performance threshold was calibrated on an Apple M5 and may need broader
  device validation.
- CUDA retains the stock implementation; no CUDA search kernel is included.
- The fixed-point representation preserves FP32 softmax support through the
  cumulative sum but does not provide higher-precision probabilities than FP32.

## Tests

- Metal Python suite: 777 passed, 3 skipped, 10,877 subtests passed.
- CPU-only categorical/export subset: 35 passed, 1 Metal-only skipped, 6
  subtests passed.
- 4,096 randomized CPU/Metal/oracle cases, including 2,048 strided cases: zero
  failures.
- Debug `-Werror` C++ suite excluding unrelated linalg failures: 246/246 passed.
- ASan C++ suite excluding linalg: 230/230 passed; dedicated uint64 boundary
  test also passed under UBSan with `halt_on_error=1`.

items.title: [BUG] ScatterAxis::vjp throws "Cannot calculate VJP with respect to indices" for computed indices (blocks autograd through MoE routing)
items.body:
## Describe the bug

`ScatterAxis::vjp` (and `Scatter::vjp`) throw `Cannot calculate VJP with respect to indices.` whenever the **index** argument of a scatter/gather-by-index op lies on the autodiff path — i.e. when the indices are *computed from* a tensor we are differentiating with respect to. Instead of contributing a **zero** cotangent for the (non-differentiable, integer) index argument, the primitive raises.

This makes `mx.grad`/`value_and_grad` fail for any graph where indices are derived from a trainable tensor. In particular it **blocks LoRA fine-tuning of quantized Mixture-of-Experts models** (the expert routing scatters/gathers by top-k indices that depend on the trainable router), e.g. GLM-5.2 (`glm_moe_dsa`) via `mlx-lm` — training crashes deterministically in the backward pass. Downstream report: ml-explore/mlx-lm (companion issue).

## Minimal reproduction

```python
import mlx.core as mx  # 0.31.2

def f(w):
    idx = mx.argsort(w, axis=1)[:, :1]                       # indices derived from w
    out = mx.put_along_axis(mx.zeros((3, 3)), idx,           # ScatterAxis
                            w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True), axis=1)
    return out.sum()

mx.grad(f)(mx.ones((3, 3)))
# ValueError: [scatter_axis] Cannot calculate VJP with respect to indices.
```

Notes:
- `mx.argmax` + `mx.take_along_axis` does **not** reproduce, because `argmax` yields a stop-gradient output, so the index never enters `argnums`. `argsort` has no VJP registered (its output is treated as differentiable and flows into the scatter's index arg), so `ScatterAxis::vjp` is called with `num == 1` and throws.

## Root cause (current `main`)

`mlx/primitives.cpp`:
- `ScatterAxis::vjp` (~L4570) handles `num == 0` (input) and `num == 2` (updates) but `throw`s for the index arg:
  ```cpp
  throw std::invalid_argument(
      "[scatter_axis] Cannot calculate VJP with respect to indices.");   // ~L4598
  ```
- `Scatter::vjp` (~L4400) does the same (`~L4486`), and `GatherMM::vjp` (`~L6013`) similarly.

The mathematically-correct behavior is a **zero** cotangent for the integer index argument (indices are non-differentiable), rather than raising — the same treatment `argsort`/`argmax` VJPs should return zero.

## Related prior work (both closed, unmerged)

- #3612 "Return zero VJPs for scatter indices" — proposed exactly this for `Scatter`; closed without merge. Does not cover `ScatterAxis`.
- #2345 "Add zero for argsort vjp" — closed without merge; would also resolve this repro at the `argsort` end.

## Proposed fix

Return a zero-valued cotangent for the index `argnum` in `Scatter::vjp`, `ScatterAxis::vjp`, and `GatherMM::vjp` (and/or register a zero VJP for `argsort`), instead of throwing. Happy to open a PR along the lines of #3612 extended to `ScatterAxis` if that direction is acceptable.

## Environment

- mlx **0.31.2**
- Python 3.12.13, macOS 26.2, Apple Silicon (M3 Ultra, 512 GB)
- Confirmed `throw` sites still present on `main` as of filing.

items.title: `mx.fast.rope` returns wrong values for batch rows > 0 when seq_len == 1 and batch > 1
items.body:
> **Note on provenance.** This was surfaced by Claude (Anthropic's Fable
> model) while working with me on an experimental entropy-sampler repo,
> and the subject matter is honestly out of my personal depth. I've
> verified it as far as I'm able with agent assistance before filing:
> the repro below is model-free, seeded, and runs in seconds; I've
> reproduced it across head dims 64/128/256 and both rope conventions,
> confirmed the downstream effect on two unrelated model families
> (including an **unquantized bf16** model, ruling out quantization),
> and traced it to a specific line in `rope.cpp` (see *Root cause*).
> Please correct anything I've mischaracterized.

**Repo:** ml-explore/mlx

## Summary

`mx.fast.rope` on a **contiguous** 4D input of shape `[B, H, 1, D]` with
`B > 1` returns corrupted values for every batch row after the first.
Row 0 is exact; rows ≥ 1 are wrong, and not by a position shift — no
single offset reproduces them, so the kernel appears to be mis-indexing
data across rows. `[B, H, 1, D]` is the standard batched single-token
decode shape, so any batched decode whose rope input materializes
contiguous is affected (see impact below).

Verified properties:

- Fires **only at seq_len == 1** with batch > 1; seq_len ≥ 2 is exact
  for every batch size tested.
- **Row 0 is always exact**; rows ≥ 1 are corrupted.
- **At `offset=0` the correct output is provably the input** (position 0
  ⇒ rotation angle 0 ⇒ identity), yet corrupted rows come back as
  **zeros** — a value the identity map cannot produce. This removes any
  "expected numerics" reading: the kernel is not miscomputing a
  rotation, it is emitting data that isn't a rotation of the input at
  all.
- **Some shapes read uninitialized memory**, not merely wrong values:
  e.g. contiguous `[4, 8, 1, 128]` bf16 has produced ~`3.5e37` in a
  corrupted row, and the set of affected `(B, H)` combinations is not
  stable — the signature of out-of-bounds / uninitialized reads.
- **Dtype-independent**: bf16, fp16, and fp32 all affected (fp32 worst
  row deviation 6.08 below), so this is an indexing bug, not precision.
- **The result depends on input strides**: a transposed *view* holding
  the same values produces the *correct* result; the contiguous copy is
  the wrong one.
- Reproduces identically through `nn.RoPE` (which calls `mx.fast.rope`).

## Environment

- mlx 0.31.2 (via pip; mlx-metal 0.31.2)
- macOS 26.5.1, Apple M4 Max, 128 GB
- Python 3.12

## Repro

```python
import mlx.core as mx

mx.random.seed(0)

def rope(x, offset=32):
    return mx.fast.rope(x, 256, traditional=False, base=10000.0,
                        scale=1.0, offset=offset)

# 1) Wrong values, only at T==1 with B>1 (contiguous input)
print("worst batch-row deviation vs the same row processed alone:")
for B in (2, 8):
    for T in (1, 2, 8):
        x = mx.contiguous(mx.random.normal((1, 16, B, T, 256))
                          .astype(mx.bfloat16)[0].transpose(1, 0, 2, 3))
        out = rope(x)  # x: contiguous [B, 16, T, 256]
        worst = max(mx.abs(out[i:i+1] - rope(mx.contiguous(x[i:i+1])))
                    .max().item() for i in range(B))
        print(f"  B={B} T={T}: {worst:.4f}")

# 2) Row 0 is correct; rows >= 1 are corrupted, and not by a position
#    shift -- no single offset reproduces them
x = mx.contiguous(mx.random.normal((8, 16, 1, 256)).astype(mx.bfloat16))
out = rope(x)
for i in (0, 1, 4):
    best = min((mx.abs(out[i:i+1] - rope(mx.contiguous(x[i:i+1]), off))
                .max().item(), off) for off in range(24, 48))
    print(f"row {i}: best-fit offset {best[1]} (requested 32), dev {best[0]:.4f}")

# 3) Result depends on strides: a transposed VIEW of the same values is
#    CORRECT, the contiguous copy is wrong
xv = mx.random.normal((1, 16, 8, 256)).astype(mx.bfloat16).transpose(2, 1, 0, 3)
a, b = rope(xv), rope(mx.contiguous(xv))
ref = mx.concatenate([rope(mx.contiguous(xv[i:i+1])) for i in range(8)])
print("view vs per-row reference:      ", mx.abs(a - ref).max().item())
print("contiguous vs per-row reference:", mx.abs(b - ref).max().item())

# 4) dtype-independent (also fp32)
x32 = mx.contiguous(mx.random.normal((8, 16, 1, 256)))
out32 = rope(x32)
worst = max(mx.abs(out32[i:i+1] - rope(mx.contiguous(x32[i:i+1])))
            .max().item() for i in range(8))
print("fp32 worst row dev:", round(worst, 4))

# 5) offset=0 is the identity (angle 0), so out MUST equal the input.
#    Row 0 does; row 1 comes back as zeros -- not a rotation of anything.
x0 = mx.array([[[[1., 2., 3., 4.]]], [[[5., 6., 7., 8.]]]])  # [2,1,1,4]
o0 = mx.fast.rope(x0, 4, traditional=False, base=10000.0, scale=1.0, offset=0)
print("offset=0 row0 (want [1,2,3,4]):", o0[0].tolist())
print("offset=0 row1 (want [5,6,7,8]):", o0[1].tolist())
```

## Observed output (mlx 0.31.2, M4 Max)

```
worst batch-row deviation vs the same row processed alone:
  B=2 T=1: 4.2188
  B=2 T=2: 0.0000
  B=2 T=8: 0.0000
  B=8 T=1: 4.2812
  B=8 T=2: 0.0000
  B=8 T=8: 0.0000
row 0: best-fit offset 32 (requested 32), dev 0.0000
row 1: best-fit offset 39 (requested 32), dev 3.2656
row 4: best-fit offset 30 (requested 32), dev 3.6094
view vs per-row reference:       0.0
contiguous vs per-row reference: 6.875
fp32 worst row dev: 6.0794
offset=0 row0 (want [1,2,3,4]): [[[1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]]]
offset=0 row1 (want [5,6,7,8]): [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]]]
```

## Root cause (host-side dispatch in `rope.cpp`)

The bug is in kernel *dispatch*, not the shader math. The single-time-step
fast-path is selected by:

```cpp
// mlx/backend/metal/rope.cpp
bool single = in.flags().row_contiguous && T == 1 && offset.size() == 1;
```

When `single` is true it launches `rope_single` with grid:

```cpp
grid_dims = MTL::Size(dims_ / 2, N, 1);   // (D/2, n_heads, 1)
```

`N` here is the product of the middle dims (n_heads); **the batch
dimension `B` is not in the grid at all**. `rope_single` therefore only
addresses the first batch matrix, and rows ≥ 1 of the freshly
`malloc`-ed output are never written — they contain uninitialized
memory (hence zeros / `3.5e37` above). This path predates batched
decode and assumes "single time step" ⇒ batch 1.

Consistent with this: anything that avoids the `single` predicate is
correct. A non-contiguous view (fails `row_contiguous`) and a per-row
offset array of length `B` (makes `offset.size() != 1`) both fall
through to the general `rope` kernel, whose grid includes batch
(`dim2 = B * ceil(N/4)`), and both return exact results:

```
scalar offset (single path) worst dev: 4.0625
array  offset (general path) worst dev: 0.0
```

**Suggested fix:** require batch 1 for the fast-path, e.g.
`single = in.flags().row_contiguous && T == 1 && B == 1 && offset.size() == 1;`
so batched decode uses the general kernel (which is already correct).

## Expected

All batch rows equal to the same row processed alone, independent of
input strides and of the other rows in the batch.

## Impact

`[B, H, 1, D]` is exactly the shape attention layers feed to rope
during **batched single-token decode**, so this is architecture-
independent: the repro above reproduces across head dims 64/128/256 and
both `traditional` conventions. In mlx-lm (0.31.3), batch>1 decode
shows the matching signature — row 0 exact, rows ≥ 1 corrupted — on
multiple model families: Gemma-4 (logits off by up to ~27, top-1 flips
on 7 of 8 rows; word salad on a quantized MoE) and Qwen3-4B in
**unquantized bf16** (rows 1–7 off by 6–15, ruling out quantization as
the cause). Filed separately against mlx-lm with repros; the two issues
are very likely the same root cause.

The failure is silent — no error, plausible-looking output — which is
what makes it dangerous: downstream it looks like "quantization
artifacts" or "sampler weirdness" rather than a kernel bug.

items.title: MLXNN.RoPE produces row-asymmetric output for byte-identical row inputs at [B>1, H, 1, D]
items.body:
## Summary

`MLXNN.RoPE` (which dispatches into `MLXFast.RoPE`) on a `[B, H, 1, D]` input where row 0 == row 1 produces row-asymmetric output. The same op on `[B, H, T, D]` with `T > 1` is row-symmetric. The same op with `B = 1` is deterministic and correct.

This blocks any straightforward `[B,1,H]` batched autoregressive decode in mlx-swift — every decoder layer's attention applies RoPE per step at `T=1`, and the resulting per-row drift compounds through the layers fast enough that argmax tokens diverge within a few decode steps.

## Minimal reproducer (no model, no quantization)

```swift
import MLX
import MLXNN
import MLXRandom

MLXRandom.seed(42)

let rope = MLXNN.RoPE(dimensions: 128, traditional: false, base: 1_000_000)

// Row-symmetric input: row 0 byte-equal to row 1.
let baseRow = MLXRandom.normal([1, 8, 1, 128])  // [1, H, T=1, D]
let input = concatenated([baseRow, baseRow], axis: 0)  // [2, H, T=1, D]

// Sanity: input rows are identical.
let i0 = input[0..<1, 0..., 0..., 0...].asArray(Float.self)
let i1 = input[1..<2, 0..., 0..., 0...].asArray(Float.self)
let inputDiff = zip(i0, i1).map { abs($0 - $1) }.max() ?? 0
assert(inputDiff == 0)

let output = rope(input, offset: 0)

let r0 = output[0..<1, 0..., 0..., 0...].asArray(Float.self)
let r1 = output[1..<2, 0..., 0..., 0...].asArray(Float.self)
let rowDiff = zip(r0, r1).map { abs($0 - $1) }.max() ?? 0

print("RoPE B=2 T=1 offset=0 row-diff: \(rowDiff)")
// Expected: 0.0
// Actual:   5.379... (varies by seed but always non-zero)
```

## Diagnostic matrix

| Shape | Op | Offset | row 0 vs row 1 maxDiff |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[2, 1, 1024]` | `quantizedMatmul` (4-bit, group 64) | — | **0.0** ✓ |
| `[2, 148, 1024]` | `quantizedMatmul` (4-bit, group 64) | — | **0.0** ✓ |
| `[2, 8, 1, 128]` | `qProj → reshape → RMSNorm → transpose` | — | **0.0** ✓ |
| `[2, 8, 1, 128]` | **`RoPE`** | **0** | **5.38** ✗ |
| `[2, 8, 1, 128]` | **`RoPE`** | **148** | **7.52** ✗ |
| `[2, 8, 2, 128]` | `RoPE` | 148 | **0.0** ✓ (T>1 control) |
| `[1, 8, 1, 128]` | `RoPE` (called twice) | 148 | **0.0** ✓ (B=1 deterministic) |

The trigger is **`B > 1` AND `T = 1`** — independent of `offset`, independent of preceding ops (the bug shows up on a freshly constructed tensor that never went through quantizedMatmul or RMSNorm).

## Why it matters

This silently corrupts any batched autoregressive decode loop in mlx-swift, because:

1. Decoder forward pass at decode step has shape `[B, H, T=1, D]` (one new query per row).
2. RoPE is applied to every layer's Q and K at `offset = current_cache_length`.
3. The per-row drift introduced by RoPE compounds through ~28 layers per step.
4. Argmax over the LM head picks different tokens for different rows within a few steps even when rows started identical.

Surface symptom: feeding two identical chunks through a batched decode loop produces correct output for row 0 and a truncated / different output for row 1.

We hit this in [soniqo/speech-swift PR ml-explore/mlx-swift-examples#453](https://github.com/soniqo/speech-swift/pull/234)'s experimental `[B,1,H]` batched decoder for Qwen3-ASR. With `B=2` and two identical 10s audio chunks, row 0 transcribes the full sentence and row 1 stops after the first few tokens. Cache layout (per-step `concatenated` vs. mlx-lm-style pre-allocated `BatchKVCache`) does not change the symptom — both fail in the same way because the upstream cause is `RoPE` itself.

## What we ruled out

- ✅ Determinism: same op, same input, run twice → byte-identical (so it's not a kernel-level race).
- ✅ Cache layout: mlx-lm-style `BatchKVCache` (pre-allocated, indexed-slice writes) does not fix it.
- ✅ Quantization: triggers without any quantized op — pure RoPE on a freshly constructed tensor reproduces.
- ✅ Position offset: `offset = 0` reproduces (~5.4 row diff), so it's not specific to non-zero positions.
- ✅ `T > 1` is fine: same op at `T = 2` is row-symmetric.
- ✅ `B = 1` is fine: same op at `B = 1` is deterministic and matches per-row B=2 row 0.

## Probable cause

A `T = 1` fast path in `MLXFast.RoPE`'s Metal kernel that doesn't broadcast / iterate the batch dim correctly. Apple's mlx core changelog mentioned `"No copy batch rope"` recently — possibly related.

## Workaround we ship

Per-row `B=1` decoder forwards (no kernel-level B amortisation). Acceptable for our 11% throughput win on token-sync batching, but blocks the larger speedup that true `[B,1,H]` would unlock.

## Environment

- macOS 26.4 (Tahoe), arm64, Apple M5 Pro
- Xcode 17 stable, Swift 6.2
- mlx-swift `0.31.3` (revision `61b9e01`)
- Reproducible against `MLXNN.RoPE` and `MLXFast.RoPE` (RoPE wraps Fast)

## Cross-references

- [mlx-lm `BatchKVCache`](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/models/cache.py) — Python pattern for batched generation. Likely also affected upstream once mlx-swift-lm wires up batched decode with quantized models.
- ["The Hidden Problem With MLX"](https://adityakarnam.com/mlx-non-determinism-apple-silicon/) — documented batch invariance failures in floating-point Metal kernels; this finding extends the picture: also `RoPE` at `T=1`, also affects models with quantized weights when surrounded by bf16 RoPE.

items.title: [BUG] `quantized_matmul` produces wrong results for GQA `expand_dims` broadcasting when M < `vector_limit`
items.body:
**Describe the bug**

`mx.quantized_matmul` produces severely wrong results when the weight tensor has a stride-0 batch dimension (from `mx.expand_dims`, used for GQA broadcasting) and M is small enough to trigger the `qmv` kernel. The error is orders of magnitude larger than the shape-dependence issue described in #3473 (max_diff up to **12.46** in real inference vs ~2e-5 for the proj case), large enough to corrupt softmax distributions and cause LLM hallucinations.

In GQA (Grouped Query Attention) with a quantized KV cache, the standard pattern is:

```python
# queries: (B, n_kv_heads, n_repeats, M, D)
# q_keys:  (B, n_kv_heads, N, D//pack_factor)  — quantized tuple
qk_e = tree_map(lambda x: mx.expand_dims(x, axis=-3), q_keys)
# qk_e[0] shape: (B, n_kv_heads, 1, N, D//pack_factor), stride-0 on dim -3
scores = mx.quantized_matmul(queries, *qk_e, transpose=True, ...)
```

`ensure_row_contiguous_matrix` (called at the top of `QuantizedMatmul::eval_gpu`) only checks the last two dimensions for row-contiguity. A weight tensor with stride-0 on a batch dimension passes through without a copy, retaining its zero stride. That stride is then forwarded verbatim to the Metal kernel via `add_strides_and_shapes`. When M < `vector_limit`, the dispatch routes to `qmv`, which does not handle stride-0 batch dimensions correctly, producing wrong output for large N (error appears at N > ~2048 and grows with cache size). The `qmm` path handles stride-0 correctly.

This is a distinct bug from the shape-dependence issue in #3473: the problem here is not fp32 non-associativity across different reduction trees, but incorrect memory access patterns in `qmv` when batch strides are zero.

**To Reproduce**

```python
import mlx.core as mx
from mlx.utils import tree_map

B, n_kv_heads, n_repeats, D = 1, 4, 4, 256
n_q_heads = n_kv_heads * n_repeats
key_bits, value_bits, group_size = 8, 4, 64

mx.random.seed(42)

def run(N, M):
    keys_f = mx.random.normal((B, n_kv_heads, N, D)).astype(mx.float16)
    values_f = mx.random.normal((B, n_kv_heads, N, D)).astype(mx.float16)
    q_keys = mx.quantize(keys_f, group_size=group_size, bits=key_bits)
    q_values = mx.quantize(values_f, group_size=group_size, bits=value_bits)
    queries = (mx.random.normal((B, n_q_heads, M, D)) * D**-0.5).astype(mx.float16)
    mx.eval(q_keys, q_values, queries)

    # reference: dequantize then float matmul
    keys_dq = mx.dequantize(*q_keys, group_size=group_size, bits=key_bits)
    values_dq = mx.dequantize(*q_values, group_size=group_size, bits=value_bits)
    qr = queries.reshape(B, n_kv_heads, n_repeats, M, D)
    s_ref = mx.softmax(qr @ keys_dq[:,:,None,:,:].transpose(0,1,2,4,3), axis=-1)
    out_ref = (s_ref @ values_dq[:,:,None,:,:]).reshape(B, n_q_heads, M, D)

    # quantized_matmul with expand_dims broadcast (GQA)
    qk_e = tree_map(lambda x: mx.expand_dims(x, axis=-3), q_keys)
    qv_e = tree_map(lambda x: mx.expand_dims(x, axis=-3), q_values)
    s_qmm = mx.softmax(mx.quantized_matmul(qr, *qk_e, transpose=True, group_size=group_size, bits=key_bits), axis=-1)
    out_qmm = mx.quantized_matmul(s_qmm, *qv_e, transpose=False, group_size=group_size, bits=value_bits).reshape(B, n_q_heads, M, D)

    mx.eval(out_ref, out_qmm)
    diff = mx.max(mx.abs(out_ref.astype(mx.float32) - out_qmm.astype(mx.float32))).item()
    print(f"N={N:5d} M={M}: max_diff={diff:.6f}")

for N in [512, 2048, 4096, 7358]:
    for M in [1, 2]:
        run(N, M)
```

Output on M4 Pro:

```
N=  512 M=1: max_diff=0.000244   # within quantization noise
N=  512 M=2: max_diff=0.000244   # ok, qmm path
N= 2048 M=1: max_diff=0.000122
N= 2048 M=2: max_diff=0.140656   # qmv triggered, error grows
N= 4096 M=1: max_diff=0.000092
N= 4096 M=2: max_diff=0.118958   # wrong
N= 7358 M=1: max_diff=0.000061
N= 7358 M=2: max_diff=0.079422   # wrong, mean_diff ~0.009
```

M=1 is always correct (qmv handles the non-broadcast single-token decode case). The bug triggers for M >= 2 combined with stride-0 batch dims and N > ~2048.

**Expected behavior**

`quantized_matmul` with a stride-0 weight tensor (GQA `expand_dims` broadcast) should produce the same result as dequantizing the weights and using standard float matmul, regardless of M.

**Desktop:**
- OS Version: macOS 26.4.1
- Version: 0.31.1 and 0.31.2

**Additional context**

In actual inference (real model, N=7358), I measured `max_diff` up to **12.46** between the `qmv` and dequantize-then-float-matmul paths in certain attention layers. The practical symptom is severely degraded generation: repetition loops, wrong task execution. The issue only manifests when a quantized KV cache is used (routing through `quantized_scaled_dot_product_attention` in mlx-lm) combined with a small-M pass such as a 2-token verification step. Without KV quantization, `mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention` is used and the bug does not trigger.

**Proposed fix**

After `ensure_row_contiguous_matrix`, check for zero strides on the batch dimensions of `w` before the kernel dispatch. If any are found, route to `qmm`, which already handles stride-0 batch dims correctly (confirmed by the reproducer: max_diff within quantization noise at M=2, N=512, where `qmm` is selected):

```cpp
// In QuantizedMatmul::eval_gpu, after ensure_row_contiguous_matrix calls:
bool has_broadcast_batch = false;
for (int i = 0; i + 2 < w.ndim(); i++) {
    if (w.strides()[i] == 0) { has_broadcast_batch = true; break; }
}
if (has_broadcast_batch) {
    qmm(x, w, scales, biases, out, transpose_, group_size_, bits_, M, N, K, d, s, mode);
    return;
}
```

This is complementary to the `MLX_NUMERICAL_STRICT_MODE` opt-in in #3473, which addresses the shape-dependence issue for contiguous tensors. The stride-0 check fires automatically with no env var and adds negligible overhead. Standard M=1 decode with contiguous weights is completely unaffected.

It may also be worth checking whether `GatherQMM::eval_gpu` is exposed to the same issue for MoE models with GQA.
